annotations.text:
Three directions, one per row. Left to right: the board (the new project home), a passage being written, the workspace.

Each row shows both themes — the direction's primary theme on the board and workspace, the other on the writing view — so you can judge both without doubling the artboards.

Every screen uses Lexend for reading and a different serif for headlines. Content is real: the same four cards, the same passage, the same three books.

A · INK & OCHRE

Your logo, taken literally. Cream paper, deep teal ink, ochre accent. Headlines in Newsreader — a contemporary editorial serif with warmth but none of Georgia's newsprint.

Views are text tabs with an underline. Cards look like paper without pretending to be paper.

Why: it is the only direction that looks like it belongs to the logo you drew, and warmth is defensible for a tool about writing.

Against: warm-on-warm is the easiest of the three to make look soft, and the board — a dense working surface — is where that risk lands.

B · STUDIO

The board is the product. Dark-first, cool neutrals, one ochre accent held back for selection and primary actions. Headlines in Instrument Serif — high contrast, unmistakably current.

Views move to a left icon rail, so the whole top bar is free and the canvas starts higher.

Why: this is what a modern canvas tool looks like, and the board is where the hours go. Dark also flatters a dense surface of pale cards.

Against: it reads as a tool rather than a writing room, and the icon rail costs you the view names until you learn them.

C · ATLAS

Structure made visible. Hairline rules instead of panels, a real ruled grid instead of dots, monospace for anything countable, and Bodoni Moda for headlines — the highest contrast of the three.

Views are a numbered row. Cards are outlined, not filled. Selection gets corner marks like a drafting handle.

Why: the most distinctive of the three by a distance, and it takes the board's coordinates seriously rather than hiding them.

Against: the riskiest. Precision can read as cold, and a novelist is not a draughtsman.
